items.stem: Which term is defined as "apparatus used to measure the rate of respiration of small organisms by their oxygen uptake"?
items.answer: Respirometer
items.markingKey: Respirometer: apparatus used to measure the rate of respiration of small organisms by their oxygen uptake.

items.stem: Explain why germinating seeds release heat.
items.answer: They respire rapidly to provide energy for growth; some energy released by respiration is lost as heat.
items.markingKey: respiration [1]; energy released as heat [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why a respirometer containing germinating seeds needs soda lime.
items.answer: Soda lime absorbs carbon dioxide released, so any change in volume is due to oxygen uptake only.
items.markingKey: absorbs CO₂ [1]; volume change = oxygen used [1] [2]

items.stem: Use the balanced equation for aerobic respiration, C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O. (a) State the number of molecules of carbon dioxide produced from 6 molecules of glucose. (b) The Mr of glucose is 180 and of CO₂ is 44. Calculate the mass of carbon dioxide released when 18 g of glucose is respired.

Use the balanced equation for aerobic respiration, C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O. (a) State the number of molecules of carbon dioxide produced from 4 molecules of glucose. (b) The Mr of glucose is 180 and of CO₂ is 44. Calculate the mass of carbon dioxide released when 90 g of glucose is respired.

Arjun set up a respirometer containing germinating peas and soda lime in a water bath, and measured the distance moved by a drop of coloured liquid in a capillary tube in 10 minutes at different temperatures. Results table. Temperature / °C: 10, 15, 20, 25, 30. Distance moved by liquid / mm, trial 1: 11, 11, 16, 22, 30; trial 2: 8, 11, 15, 23, 31; trial 3: 8, 11, 15, 22, 32. (a) Describe the trend shown by the results. (b) State the type of graph you would draw to display these results and what you would plot on each axis.
items.answer: (a) As the temperature increases, the distance moved by liquid increases (from 8 to 31). (b) A line graph: temperature on the x-axis and mean distance moved by liquid on the y-axis.
items.markingKey: (a) correct overall pattern [1]; data quoted with units / turning point given [1] [2] (b) line graph (continuous independent variable) [1]; temperature on x-axis and distance moved by liquid on y-axis [1] [2]

items.stem: Freya set up a respirometer containing germinating peas and soda lime in a water bath, and measured the distance moved by a drop of coloured liquid in a capillary tube in 10 minutes at different temperatures. Results table. Temperature / °C: 5, 10, 20, 30, 40. Distance moved by liquid / mm, trial 1: 6, 9, 18, 37, 70; trial 2: 6, 9, 17, 53, 73; trial 3: 6, 9, 18, 35, 70. (a) Identify the independent variable and the dependent variable in this investigation. (b) State two variables that should be kept constant in this investigation.
items.answer: (a) Independent: temperature; dependent: distance moved by liquid. (b) Mass / number of peas; mass of soda lime.
items.markingKey: (a) independent variable = temperature [1]; dependent variable = distance moved by liquid [1] [2] (b) Any two from: mass / number of peas; mass of soda lime; time allowed; diameter of capillary tube; time allowed to equilibrate [2]

items.stem: Kenji set up a respirometer containing germinating peas and soda lime in a water bath, and measured the distance moved by a drop of coloured liquid in a capillary tube in 10 minutes at different temperatures. Results table. Temperature / °C: 15, 20, 25, 30, 35. Distance moved by liquid / mm, trial 1: 11, 16, 23, 33, 44; trial 2: 11, 16, 23, 33, 44; trial 3: 11, 16, 23, 32, 27. (a) Explain the results. (b) State the type of graph you would draw to display these results and what you would plot on each axis.
items.answer: (a) As temperature increases, the enzymes controlling respiration work faster (more kinetic energy, more collisions), so more oxygen is used; CO₂ is absorbed by soda lime so the volume of gas falls and the liquid moves further. (b) A line graph: temperature on the x-axis and mean distance moved by liquid on the y-axis.
items.markingKey: (a) enzymes / kinetic energy [1]; more oxygen used [1]; CO₂ absorbed so gas volume falls [1] [3] (b) line graph (continuous independent variable) [1]; temperature on x-axis and distance moved by liquid on y-axis [1] [2]

items.stem: Which is the correct definition of the term "aerobic respiration"?
options: The chemical reactions in cells that use oxygen to break down nutrient molecules to release energy.
All the chemical reactions that take place in an organism.
Apparatus used to measure the rate of respiration of small organisms by their oxygen uptake.
The organelles in which most of the reactions of aerobic respiration take place.
items.answer: The chemical reactions in cells that use oxygen to break down nutrient molecules to release energy.
items.markingKey: Aerobic respiration: the chemical reactions in cells that use oxygen to break down nutrient molecules to release energy.

items.stem: Which is the balanced equation for aerobic respiration?
items.answer: C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O
items.markingKey: Glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water (energy released).

items.stem: Explain why the control in a vacuum-flask experiment uses boiled seeds washed in disinfectant.
items.answer: Boiled seeds are dead and cannot respire; disinfectant kills microorganisms that would respire and release heat, so any temperature rise in the test flask is due to the seeds.
items.markingKey: dead seeds [1]; microorganisms killed [1] [2]

items.stem: For which use of energy from respiration is a runner sprinting an example?
options: muscle contraction / movement of the flagellum
items.answer: muscle contraction
items.markingKey: A runner sprinting: energy used for muscle contraction.

items.stem: Omar placed germinating mung beans in vacuum flask A and boiled, disinfected mung beans in flask B. Both started at 20 °C. After 2 days, flask A was at 29.6 °C and flask B was still at 20 °C. (a) Explain the temperature rise in flask A. (b) Explain why the flasks were plugged with cotton wool rather than sealed with a rubber bung.
items.answer: (a) The germinating beans respire aerobically, releasing energy; some energy is released as heat, and the vacuum flask reduces heat loss. (b) Cotton wool lets oxygen in for aerobic respiration and carbon dioxide out, while still reducing heat loss.
items.markingKey: (a) respiration [1]; heat released [1]; insulation [1] [3] (b) [2]

items.stem: Which is the correct definition of the term "lactic acid"?
options: Anaerobic respiration in yeast, producing ethanol and carbon dioxide.
The extra oxygen needed after exercise to break down the lactic acid built up during anaerobic respiration.
The product of anaerobic respiration in muscles.
The alcohol produced by anaerobic respiration in yeast.
items.answer: The product of anaerobic respiration in muscles.
items.markingKey: Lactic acid: the product of anaerobic respiration in muscles.

items.stem: Explain why a sprinter continues to breathe heavily after a race.
items.answer: During the sprint muscles respired anaerobically, producing lactic acid; extra oxygen (the oxygen debt) is needed to break down the lactic acid in the liver, so heart and breathing rates stay high.
items.markingKey: anaerobic during race [1]; lactic acid [1]; oxygen debt repaid / lactic acid broken down [1] [3]

items.stem: Explain why muscles become fatigued (painful) during long vigorous exercise.
items.answer: Not enough oxygen reaches muscles, so they respire anaerobically; lactic acid builds up, causing fatigue / cramp.
items.markingKey: insufficient oxygen [1]; lactic acid build-up [1] [2]

items.stem: Tomás mixed yeast with sugar solution at different temperatures and counted the bubbles of carbon dioxide released through a delivery tube in 2 minutes. Results table. Temperature / °C: 20, 30, 40, 50, 60. Number of bubbles / bubbles in 2 min, trial 1: 9, 34, 42, 16, 1; trial 2: 9, 32, 41, 17, 2; trial 3: 8, 33, 39, 17, 2. Calculate the mean number of bubbles at 60 °C, ignoring any anomalous result.
items.answer: 2 bubbles in 2 min

items.stem: Zara mixed yeast with sugar solution at different temperatures and counted the bubbles of carbon dioxide released through a delivery tube in 2 minutes. Results table. Temperature / °C: 10, 20, 30, 40, 50. Number of bubbles / bubbles in 2 min, trial 1: 1, 8, 33, 38, 16; trial 2: 1, 8, 32, 38, 15; trial 3: 1, 8, 30, 37, 15. (a) Describe the trend shown by the results. (b) Suggest one way to improve this investigation.
items.answer: (a) The number of bubbles increases as the temperature rises to 40 °C, which gives the highest value, then decreases. (b) Collect the gas in a gas syringe or measuring cylinder to measure volume.
items.markingKey: (a) correct overall pattern [1]; data quoted with units / turning point given [1] [2] (b) Any one from: collect the gas in a gas syringe or measuring cylinder to measure volume; add a layer of oil over the mixture to keep it anaerobic; repeat each test more times and calculate a mean (to improve reliability); test more values of the temperature (smaller intervals), especially near the turning point / extremes [1]

items.stem: Freya mixed yeast with sugar solution at different temperatures and counted the bubbles of carbon dioxide released through a delivery tube in 2 minutes. Results table. Temperature / °C: 15, 25, 35, 45, 55. Number of bubbles / bubbles in 2 min, trial 1: 3, 18, 38, 28, 10; trial 2: 3, 18, 41, 29, 7; trial 3: 3, 17, 40, 28, 7. (a) Identify the independent variable and the dependent variable in this investigation. (b) Calculate the mean number of bubbles at 55 °C, ignoring any anomalous result.
items.answer: (a) Independent: temperature; dependent: number of bubbles. (b) 7 bubbles in 2 min
items.markingKey: (a) independent variable = temperature [1]; dependent variable = number of bubbles [1] [2] (b) (7 + 7) ÷ 2 [1] = 7 bubbles in 2 min [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain how lactic acid is removed after exercise.
items.answer: It diffuses into the blood and is carried to the liver, where it is broken down using oxygen (aerobic respiration).
items.markingKey: blood transport to liver [1]; broken down with oxygen [1] [2]

items.stem: An athlete in Singapore had a blood lactic acid concentration of 1.0 mmol/dm³ at rest and 8.6 mmol/dm³ immediately after a 400 m race. It took 40 minutes to return to the resting level. (a) Calculate the percentage increase. (b) Explain why lactic acid concentration increased during the race.
items.answer: (a) 760% (b) Oxygen could not be delivered fast enough, so muscles respired anaerobically, producing lactic acid.
items.markingKey: (a) (8.6 − 1.0) ÷ 1.0 × 100 = 760% [2] (b) insufficient oxygen [1]; anaerobic respiration produces lactic acid [1] [4]

items.stem: An athlete in Cape Town had a blood lactic acid concentration of 1.0 mmol/dm³ at rest and 12.9 mmol/dm³ immediately after a 400 m race. It took 60 minutes to return to the resting level. (a) Calculate the percentage increase. (b) Explain why lactic acid concentration increased during the race. (c) Calculate the mean rate of fall of lactic acid during recovery. (d) Explain how it is removed.
items.answer: (a) 1190% (b) Oxygen could not be delivered fast enough, so muscles respired anaerobically, producing lactic acid. (c) 0.198 mmol/dm³ per min (d) Carried in blood to the liver and broken down using oxygen (oxygen debt).
items.markingKey: (a) (12.9 − 1.0) ÷ 1.0 × 100 = 1190% [2] (b) insufficient oxygen [1]; anaerobic respiration produces lactic acid [1] (c) (12.9 − 1.0) ÷ 60 = 0.198 [1] (d) liver [1]; aerobic breakdown / oxygen debt [1] [7]

items.stem: Arjun mixed yeast with sugar solution at different temperatures and counted the bubbles of carbon dioxide released through a delivery tube in 2 minutes. Results table. Temperature / °C: 10, 20, 30, 40, 50. Number of bubbles / bubbles in 2 min, trial 1: 1, 9, 35, 42, 18; trial 2: 1, 9, 49, 44, 18; trial 3: 1, 9, 34, 42, 18. (a) Explain the results. (b) Suggest one way to improve this investigation. (c) Describe a test to show that the gas is carbon dioxide.
items.answer: (a) Up to about 35–40 °C the enzymes in yeast respiration work faster (more kinetic energy and collisions), so more CO₂ is released; above that the enzymes are denatured and the rate falls. (b) Collect the gas in a gas syringe or measuring cylinder to measure volume. (c) Bubble it through limewater, which turns milky / cloudy.
items.markingKey: (a) faster enzyme activity [1]; optimum [1]; denaturation above optimum [1] [3] (b) Any one from: collect the gas in a gas syringe or measuring cylinder to measure volume; add a layer of oil over the mixture to keep it anaerobic; repeat each test more times and calculate a mean (to improve reliability); test more values of the temperature (smaller intervals), especially near the turning point / extremes [1] (c) [2]

items.stem: Which is the correct definition of the term "alveolus"?
options: A small branching tube in the lung ending in alveoli.
One of two tubes branching from the trachea into each lung.
The windpipe, supported by rings of cartilage, carrying air to the bronchi.
A tiny air sac in the lungs where gas exchange takes place.
items.answer: A tiny air sac in the lungs where gas exchange takes place.
items.markingKey: Alveolus: a tiny air sac in the lungs where gas exchange takes place.

items.stem: Explain why exhaled air contains less oxygen and more carbon dioxide than inhaled air.
items.answer: Oxygen diffuses from alveoli into the blood to be used in respiration; carbon dioxide produced by respiration diffuses from the blood into the alveoli.
items.markingKey: oxygen absorbed for respiration [1]; CO₂ released from respiration [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why exhaled air is warmer and wetter than inhaled air.
items.answer: Air is warmed by the body and water evaporates from the moist alveolar surfaces into the air.

items.stem: Inhaled air contains 21% oxygen and 0.04% carbon dioxide. Exhaled air contains 16.6% oxygen and 3.7% carbon dioxide. (a) Calculate the percentage decrease in oxygen. (b) Calculate how many times greater the carbon dioxide concentration is in exhaled air.
items.answer: (a) 21% (b) 92 times

items.stem: Inhaled air contains 21% oxygen and 0.04% carbon dioxide. Exhaled air contains 15.9% oxygen and 3.8% carbon dioxide. (a) Calculate the percentage decrease in oxygen. (b) Calculate how many times greater the carbon dioxide concentration is in exhaled air. (c) Explain these changes.
items.answer: (a) 24.3% (b) 95 times (c) Oxygen diffuses into the blood and is used in respiration; carbon dioxide from respiration diffuses into the alveoli.

items.stem: A doctor in Istanbul compares lung tissue from a non-smoker and a long-term smoker with emphysema. The total alveolar surface area is about 70 m² in the non-smoker and 35 m² in the smoker. (a) Describe how the cilia and mucus normally protect the lungs, and how smoking affects them. (b) Name two other components of tobacco smoke and state their effects.
items.answer: (a) Mucus traps pathogens and dust; cilia sweep it up and out. Smoke paralyses / destroys cilia, so mucus builds up, causing coughing and infections. (b) Nicotine: addictive, raises heart rate; carbon monoxide: combines with haemoglobin, reducing oxygen transport; tar: carcinogen.
items.markingKey: (a) normal function [1]; effect of smoking [1] [2] (b) two components with effects [2]

items.stem: Why is the trachea supported by rings of cartilage?
options: To keep it open so air can flow
items.answer: To keep it open so air can flow
items.markingKey: Cartilage prevents collapse when pressure falls during inhalation.

items.stem: Inhaled air contains 21% oxygen and exhaled air contains 15.9%. What percentage of the inhaled oxygen is absorbed? (percentage of oxygen removed = change ÷ inhaled × 100)
Describe how the gills of a fish are adapted for efficient gas exchange.
items.answer: Many filaments and lamellae give a large surface area; thin; dense capillaries; water flows over continuously.
items.markingKey: three features linked to fast diffusion [3]

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "the volume of air breathed in or out in one normal breath"?
items.answer: Tidal volume
items.markingKey: Tidal volume: the volume of air breathed in or out in one normal breath.

items.stem: Explain how air is drawn into the lungs.
items.answer: External intercostals contract, raising the ribs; diaphragm contracts and flattens; volume of the thorax increases and pressure falls below atmospheric pressure, so air flows in.
items.markingKey: muscles contract [1]; volume increases [1]; pressure falls / air flows in [1] [3]

items.stem: Explain why breathing rate stays high for some time after exercise.
items.answer: Carbon dioxide concentration is still high and oxygen debt must be repaid to break down lactic acid, so the brain keeps breathing rate high.
items.markingKey: CO₂ still high [1]; oxygen debt / lactic acid [1] [2]

items.stem: Samuel measured the breathing rate of a student at rest and at the end of each minute of running on a treadmill at increasing speed. Results table. Time running / min: 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5. Breathing rate / breaths/min, trial 1: 14, 24, 31, 34, 34, 37; trial 2: 14, 24, 30, 33, 35, 36; trial 3: 14, 25, 31, 34, 35, 37. Identify the independent variable and the dependent variable in this investigation.
items.answer: Independent: time running; dependent: breathing rate.
items.markingKey: independent variable = time running [1]; dependent variable = breathing rate [1] [2]

items.stem: Omar measured the breathing rate of a student at rest and at the end of each minute of running on a treadmill at increasing speed. Results table. Time running / min: 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5. Breathing rate / breaths/min, trial 1: 13, 26, 31, 34, 21, 35; trial 2: 14, 25, 31, 33, 36, 35; trial 3: 14, 25, 31, 33, 35, 37. (a) Identify the anomalous result in the table and state what should be done with it. (b) Suggest one way to improve this investigation.
items.answer: (a) Trial 1 at 4 min (21 breaths/min); it should be ignored when calculating the mean (or repeated). (b) Use several students and calculate a mean.
items.markingKey: (a) trial 1 at 4 min identified [1]; ignore / repeat it [1] [2] (b) Any one from: use several students and calculate a mean; measure depth of breathing as well, using a spirometer; repeat each test more times and calculate a mean (to improve reliability); test more values of the time running (smaller intervals), especially near the turning point / extremes [1]

items.stem: Priya measured the breathing rate of a student at rest and at the end of each minute of running on a treadmill at increasing speed. Results table. Time running / min: 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5. Breathing rate / breaths/min, trial 1: 8, 25, 30, 34, 36, 37; trial 2: 14, 25, 32, 35, 35, 37; trial 3: 14, 25, 32, 34, 37, 36. (a) Identify the independent variable and the dependent variable in this investigation. (b) Describe the trend shown by the results.
items.answer: (a) Independent: time running; dependent: breathing rate. (b) As the time running increases, the breathing rate increases and then levels off at about 4 min.
items.markingKey: (a) independent variable = time running [1]; dependent variable = breathing rate [1] [2] (b) correct overall pattern [1]; data quoted with units / turning point given [1] [2]

items.stem: Jonas measured the breathing rate of a student at rest and at the end of each minute of running on a treadmill at increasing speed. Results table. Time running / min: 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5. Breathing rate / breaths/min, trial 1: 14, 25, 30, 34, 35, 37; trial 2: 14, 26, 32, 33, 36, 36; trial 3: 14, 36, 31, 33, 35, 37. (a) State two variables that should be kept constant in this investigation. (b) State the type of graph you would draw to display these results and what you would plot on each axis.
items.answer: (a) Same student; temperature of the room. (b) A line graph: time running on the x-axis and mean breathing rate on the y-axis.
items.markingKey: (a) Any two from: same student; temperature of the room; method of counting breaths (same time interval); treadmill gradient [2] (b) line graph (continuous independent variable) [1]; time running on x-axis and breathing rate on y-axis [1] [2]

items.stem: Leila measured the breathing rate of a student at rest and at the end of each minute of running on a treadmill at increasing speed. Results table. Time running / min: 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5. Breathing rate / breaths/min, trial 1: 15, 27, 35, 39, 40, 42; trial 2: 14, 39, 36, 37, 41, 41; trial 3: 14, 26, 35, 39, 41, 42. (a) Describe the trend shown by the results. (b) Explain the results.
items.answer: (a) As the time running increases, the breathing rate increases and then levels off at about 4 min. (b) Running muscles respire faster and produce more CO₂; the brain detects the higher CO₂ concentration and increases breathing rate (and depth) to remove CO₂ and supply more oxygen. The rate levels off as supply meets demand.
items.markingKey: (a) correct overall pattern [1]; data quoted with units / turning point given [1] [2] (b) more respiration / CO₂ [1]; brain detects CO₂ [1]; more O₂ supplied / CO₂ removed [1] [3]

items.stem: Explain how the increase in carbon dioxide during exercise leads to deeper and faster breathing.
items.answer: More CO₂ is produced by respiring muscles; the brain detects the increased CO₂ concentration in the blood and sends impulses to the intercostal muscles and diaphragm to contract faster and more strongly.
items.markingKey: CO₂ rises [1]; detected by brain [1]; impulses to muscles [1] [3]

items.stem: Explain how exhalation happens at rest.
items.answer: The external intercostals and diaphragm relax; the ribs move down and in and the diaphragm domes up; thorax volume decreases, pressure increases above atmospheric and air is forced out.
items.markingKey: relaxation [1]; volume decreases / pressure increases [1] [2]

items.stem: Daniel says: "Air is sucked into the lungs because the lungs expand by themselves." Explain whether Daniel is correct.
items.answer: The intercostal muscles and diaphragm increase the volume of the thorax, lowering the pressure so air flows in.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error / statement is incorrect; 1 mark: The intercostal muscles and diaphragm increase the volume of the thorax, lowering the pressure so air flows in. [2]

items.stem: At rest a person takes 14 breaths per minute with a tidal volume of 0.6 dm³. During exercise this changes to 30 breaths per minute and 2.5 dm³. (a) Calculate the volume of air breathed per minute at rest and during exercise. (b) Calculate the percentage increase.
items.answer: (a) 8.4 dm³/min and 75 dm³/min (b) 793%

items.stem: Freya measured the breathing rate of a student at rest and at the end of each minute of running on a treadmill at increasing speed. Results table. Time running / min: 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5. Breathing rate / breaths/min, trial 1: 14, 26, 34, 37, 39, 41; trial 2: 14, 28, 35, 22, 38, 41; trial 3: 14, 26, 35, 39, 39, 41. (a) Identify the independent variable and the dependent variable in this investigation. (b) Identify the anomalous result in the table and state what should be done with it. (c) Each breath at 5 minutes had a volume of 1.8 dm³. Calculate the volume of air breathed per minute at 5 minutes.
items.answer: (a) Independent: time running; dependent: breathing rate. (b) Trial 2 at 3 min (22 breaths/min); it should be ignored when calculating the mean (or repeated). (c) 73.8 dm³/min
items.markingKey: (a) independent variable = time running [1]; dependent variable = breathing rate [1] [2] (b) trial 2 at 3 min identified [1]; ignore / repeat it [1] [2] (c) 41 × 1.8 [1] = 73.8 dm³/min [1] [2]

items.stem: Which process in the body does not use energy from respiration?
options: Diffusion of oxygen into the blood
items.answer: Diffusion of oxygen into the blood
items.markingKey: Diffusion is passive; muscle contraction, protein synthesis and active transport all need energy.

items.stem: Explain why cells in the body need a continuous supply of oxygen and glucose.
items.answer: Aerobic respiration needs both to release energy continuously for processes such as muscle contraction, active transport and protein synthesis.
items.markingKey: reactants of respiration [1]; continuous energy needs [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why respiration is described as a series of enzyme-controlled reactions.
items.answer: Each step is catalysed by a specific enzyme, so the rate depends on temperature and pH like other enzyme reactions.
items.markingKey: enzymes catalyse steps [1]; affected by temperature / pH [1] [2]

items.stem: Ines set up a respirometer containing germinating peas and soda lime in a water bath, and measured the distance moved by a drop of coloured liquid in a capillary tube in 10 minutes at different temperatures. Results table. Temperature / °C: 15, 20, 25, 30, 35. Distance moved by liquid / mm, trial 1: 11, 14, 20, 30, 42; trial 2: 11, 14, 22, 29, 41; trial 3: 10, 14, 21, 29, 43. Calculate the mean distance moved by liquid at 20 °C.
items.answer: 14 mm

items.stem: State how energy from respiration is used in each case: (i) cells in the skin dividing to repair a cut (ii) a runner sprinting.
items.answer: (i) cell division (ii) muscle contraction
items.markingKey: (i) cell division [1]; (ii) muscle contraction [1] [2]

items.stem: Describe aerobic respiration and explain how the energy released is used in the human body.
items.answer: Glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water in mitochondria, catalysed by enzymes, releasing energy. Uses: muscle contraction, protein synthesis, cell division, active transport, growth, nerve impulses, maintaining body temperature.
items.markingKey: equation [2]; mitochondria / enzymes [1]; three uses [3] [6]

items.stem: What are the products of anaerobic respiration in yeast?
items.answer: Ethanol and carbon dioxide
items.markingKey: Glucose → ethanol + carbon dioxide.

items.stem: Explain why yeast is used in bread making.
items.answer: Yeast respires anaerobically in the dough, producing carbon dioxide gas which forms bubbles and makes the dough rise; ethanol evaporates during baking.
items.markingKey: CO₂ produced [1]; dough rises [1] [2]

items.stem: Arjun mixed yeast with sugar solution at different temperatures and counted the bubbles of carbon dioxide released through a delivery tube in 2 minutes. Results table. Temperature / °C: 20, 30, 40, 50, 60. Number of bubbles / bubbles in 2 min, trial 1: 7, 29, 34, 14, 2; trial 2: 7, 27, 34, 15, 2; trial 3: 7, 29, 34, 14, 2. Identify the independent variable and the dependent variable in this investigation.
items.answer: Independent: temperature; dependent: number of bubbles.
items.markingKey: independent variable = temperature [1]; dependent variable = number of bubbles [1] [2]

items.stem: A baker in Istanbul mixes yeast, flour, sugar and warm water to make dough, then leaves it in a warm place for an hour before baking. (a) Explain why the dough rises. (b) Compare anaerobic respiration in yeast and in human muscle.
items.answer: (a) Yeast respires anaerobically, producing carbon dioxide gas that is trapped as bubbles in the dough. (b) Both release less energy than aerobic and use no oxygen; yeast produces ethanol and CO₂, muscle produces lactic acid only.
items.markingKey: (a) [2] (b) similarity [1]; difference in products [1] [2]

items.stem: Which term is defined as "the voice box at the top of the trachea"?
items.answer: Larynx
items.markingKey: Larynx: the voice box at the top of the trachea.

items.stem: Explain how the alveoli are adapted for efficient gas exchange.
items.answer: Millions of alveoli give a huge surface area; walls one cell thick give short diffusion distance; dense capillary network and ventilation maintain steep concentration gradients; moist lining dissolves gases.
items.markingKey: any three [3]

items.stem: Inhaled air contains 21% oxygen and 0.04% carbon dioxide. Exhaled air contains 16.1% oxygen and 4.3% carbon dioxide. (a) Calculate the percentage decrease in oxygen. (b) Calculate how many times greater the carbon dioxide concentration is in exhaled air.
Describe the structure of the human breathing system and explain how the alveoli are adapted for gas exchange.
items.answer: Larynx, trachea with cartilage rings, bronchi, bronchioles, alveoli; ribs, intercostal muscles, diaphragm. Alveoli: large surface area, thin walls, capillaries, moist, ventilation maintains gradient.
items.markingKey: structures named in order [2]; cartilage / ribs / muscles [1]; three adaptations [3] [6]

items.stem: A student in Kuala Lumpur states: "The diaphragm moves up during inhalation." Explain why this statement is incorrect.
items.answer: The diaphragm contracts and flattens (moves down) during inhalation.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error / statement is incorrect; 1 mark: The diaphragm contracts and flattens (moves down) during inhalation. [2]

items.stem: A student in Nairobi states: "Air is sucked into the lungs because the lungs expand by themselves." Explain why this statement is incorrect.
items.answer: The intercostal muscles and diaphragm increase the volume of the thorax, lowering the pressure so air flows in.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error / statement is incorrect; 1 mark: The intercostal muscles and diaphragm increase the volume of the thorax, lowering the pressure so air flows in. [2]

items.stem: At rest a person takes 16 breaths per minute with a tidal volume of 0.6 dm³. During exercise this changes to 36 breaths per minute and 2.5 dm³. (a) Calculate the volume of air breathed per minute at rest and during exercise. (b) Calculate the percentage increase.

items.stem: A teacher demonstrates breathing using a bell jar model: balloons attached to a Y-tube represent the lungs, the bell jar represents the thorax, and a rubber sheet at the bottom represents the diaphragm. (a) Describe and explain what happens to the balloons when the rubber sheet is pulled down. (b) State one way in which the model is not like the real thorax. (c) Explain why pressure changes cause air to move. (d) Describe how forced exhalation differs from exhalation at rest.
items.answer: (a) They inflate: the volume inside the jar increases, pressure falls below atmospheric, so air flows into the balloons. (b) It has no ribs or intercostal muscles; the walls cannot move; the diaphragm is pulled, not contracted; balloons are not alveoli. (c) Air moves from a region of higher pressure to lower pressure. (d) At rest exhalation is passive (muscles relax); in forced exhalation the internal intercostals and abdominal muscles contract to push air out.
items.markingKey: (a) inflate [1]; volume up / pressure down [1] [2] (b) [1] (c) [1] (d) [2]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Explain why exhaled air contains less oxygen and more carbon dioxide than inhaled air. (b) Explain why smoking damages the gas exchange system.
items.answer: (a) Oxygen diffuses from alveoli into the blood to be used in respiration; carbon dioxide produced by respiration diffuses from the blood into the alveoli. (b) Tar paralyses cilia and causes mucus to build up (bronchitis); smoke damages alveolar walls, reducing surface area (emphysema); tar contains carcinogens (lung cancer).
items.markingKey: (a) oxygen absorbed for respiration [1]; CO₂ released from respiration [1] [2] (b) any two effects explained [2]

items.stem: A doctor in Nairobi compares lung tissue from a non-smoker and a long-term smoker with emphysema. The total alveolar surface area is about 75 m² in the non-smoker and 38 m² in the smoker. (a) Calculate the percentage reduction in surface area. (b) Describe how the cilia and mucus normally protect the lungs, and how smoking affects them. (c) Name two other components of tobacco smoke and state their effects.
items.answer: (a) 49.3% (b) Mucus traps pathogens and dust; cilia sweep it up and out. Smoke paralyses / destroys cilia, so mucus builds up, causing coughing and infections. (c) Nicotine: addictive, raises heart rate; carbon monoxide: combines with haemoglobin, reducing oxygen transport; tar: carcinogen.
items.markingKey: (a) (75 − 38) ÷ 75 × 100 [1] = 49.3% [1] [2] (b) normal function [1]; effect of smoking [1] [2] (c) two components with effects [2]

items.stem: Explain how the diaphragm and intercostal muscles bring about inhalation and exhalation, and how breathing changes during exercise.
items.answer: Inhale: external intercostals contract, ribs up/out; diaphragm contracts, flattens; volume up, pressure down, air in. Exhale: relax, volume down, pressure up, air out; internal intercostals in forced exhalation. Exercise: more CO₂ detected by brain; faster and deeper breathing.
